Human-generated reference descriptions serve as the gold standard for evaluating image description systems, which typically rely on language models. However, research has shown that these descriptions often contain information not present in the image, posing challenges for assessing these systems. To address this, our team explored alternative methods using human-generated descriptions as the basis for evaluating image description models. We conducted an experiment where humans were asked to determine whether specific details in descriptions corresponded to actual features in an image or resulted from the reference description's context. We found that humans are capable of distinguishing between image-based and context-based information with a high degree of accuracy. Our findings suggest that, in certain cases, humans can effectively assess image description models by analyzing the relationship between reference descriptions and images. This research has implications for developing more accurate methods of evaluating image description models and could be applied to other visual perception tasks, such as describing videos and videos of videos. This article investigates the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based IWGT systems, focusing on the achievable rates and optimal waveforming strategies. For SISO-OFDM, we derive the maximum achievable rate and demonstrate that it surpasses the sum of individual rates for data and power. Similarly, we derive the maximum rate for MISO-OFDM and observe that it also exceeds the product of data and power rates. To analyze the rate gap, we introduce extrinsic mutual information and calculate its average value for SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM under AWGN and fading channels. Numerical results under AWGN and fading environments demonstrate that IWGT with MISO-OFDM outperforms the standard multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) communication. Additionally, we compare IWGT with MISO-OFDM to MISO waveforming and show its superiority in both scenarios. To facilitate IWGT with MISO-OFDM, we propose a practical scheme based on lattice reduction and evaluate its performance. Numerical results under AWGN and fading environments demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed scheme. All code used in this research is available at: https://github.com/authorX/IWGTCode.

Furthermore, the findings provide valuable insights into the reaction dynamics of turbulent jet flames, revealing a critical minimum frequency required for instability to occur. This minimum frequency is found to be directly related to the flame's stability, with higher frequencies leading to growing oscillations and lower frequencies resulting in damped oscillations. The research findings are expected to contribute significantly to the development of linear models for predicting combustion instability in complex, three-dimensional configurations. For graphs with a finite number of vertices, we've adapted and expanded upon existing methods to establish concise representations of vertex identities in reduced metric and shortened metric dimensions. Our approaches involve using distances between vertices and their projections onto a dimension subset, which we then translate into a concise format suitable for analysis. This concise representation enables us to determine the minimum size required for both reduced metric and shortened metric dimensions. In doing so, we derive exact values for shortened metric dimension in specific graph types, including grids, circles, and regular polyhedra, and provide general construction instructions for achieving the optimal dimension size in any graph. Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between reduced metric and shortened metric dimensions and establish their equivalence in graphs with a distance matrix of full rank. Lastly, we explore the connection between reduced metric dimension and resolving sets, delving into scenarios where a set that embodies the reduced metric dimension also serves as a resolving set and vice versa. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of graph dimension theory and its applications, particularly in biometrics and data identification, and offer valuable insights for researchers seeking to apply these theoretical frameworks in various biological and physical models. Our results also provide a foundation for investigating more complex dimensional properties, such as long-dimensional metrics, in various graph models. In addition, we present a range of open questions to facilitate future research in this area of graph theory. Our results are available on the arXiv server at http://arXiv.org.

This discrepancy could be particularly significant for gas reservoirs within massive halos, as well as those around massive galaxies. To account for non-equilibrium effects, we propose a new method involving the analysis of line ratios, which can be observed through submillimeter spectrographs like JWST. By applying this approach to data from the ALMA and HERA surveys, we see promising possibilities for better understanding gas reservoir temperatures and their relationship with the surrounding environment. This new perspective may also provide valuable insights into the dynamics of gas reservoirs and the formation of galaxies.

Language models have been successful in text processing tasks, thanks to their massive size and the sophisticated methods used to train them. As a result, they have the potential to leverage external knowledge effectively, much like human experts. To tap into this potential, I propose a novel framework called SKILL, which integrates structured information directly into language models during training. This framework overcomes the limitations of pre-trained models and enables language models to draw upon vast amounts of information that is not accessible through typical interface methods. Our experiments with the SABER framework and three structured data sources (DBpedia, Freebase, and Wikidata) demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach. By incorporating structured information into language models, we observed significant improvements in performance compared to standard models, as well as the ability to execute complex queries and reason about data. For instance, we found that the models generated through the SKILL framework excelled in tests that evaluated knowledge about famous paintings, identifying 92.1% of their artists, in contrast to 78.5% achieved by standard models. In distributed linear bandits, learning is hindered by a curse of dimensionality, particularly when the action space is high-dimensional. To address this challenge, we propose a situational linear bandit model where actions are defined by contexts and situational information is provided by situations. Compared to an ideal situation selection method, SAUCB incurs a regret of order O(\sqrt{T} \times (d \times K/\Delta_{min}^2) in the average case, and O(T \times (d \times K/\Delta_{min}^2) in the worst case, where T denotes time steps, d denotes dimension of situational information, K denotes number of situations, and \Delta_{min} denotes minimum gap between the optimal action and second-best action. We also conduct situational learning, and our analysis demonstrates that SAUCB leads to situation-aware UCB with O(\sqrt{T}) regret in the average case, and O(T) regret in the worst case, after situation learning converges. We further conduct an experiment that demonstrates the efficacy of SAUCB. We also provide a scenario in which situation-aware UCB with a linear model is not applicable, and situation-aware UCB is feasible when the situation-aware UCB with a linear model is applicable in reverse situations.
